title: Water & Feeding

learn.summary: More garden plants die from watering mistakes than anything else — usually too much, too shallow, or too often. The rule for established plants is deep and infrequent: about 1 inch of water per week including rain, delivered to the soil, not the leaves. Feeding matters far less than soil health, and overfeeding causes as many problems as underfeeding.

do: Set an empty tuna can in the garden while you water and time how long it takes to fill one inch — that is your weekly watering benchmark

children.title: Deep Watering

learn.summary: Shallow daily sprinkles train roots to stay near the surface where they cook in summer; deep weekly soaks push roots down 6-12 inches where moisture is stable. Water early morning to cut evaporation and give leaves time to dry, which reduces disease. Check before watering: finger 2 inches into the soil — if it is moist, wait.

do: Before every watering this week, do the 2-inch finger test and log how many scheduled waterings you actually skipped

children.title: Drainage

learn.summary: Roots need oxygen; waterlogged soil suffocates them, and root rot looks deceptively like drought — wilting despite wet soil. Test drainage with a percolation test: dig a 12-inch hole, fill with water, and time it — draining slower than 1 inch per hour means trouble. Fix with raised beds, organic matter, or moisture-loving plant choices, not gravel in the bottom of holes.

do: Run a percolation test this weekend in the spot where plants struggle most: 12-inch hole, fill with water, measure the drop each hour

children.title: Mulching

learn.summary: A 2-3 inch layer of organic mulch (wood chips, straw, shredded leaves) cuts evaporation dramatically, suppresses weeds, buffers soil temperature, and feeds the soil as it breaks down. Keep mulch 2-3 inches back from stems and trunks — piled-up "mulch volcanoes" rot bark and invite rodents. Refresh once a year.

do: Mulch one bed 2-3 inches deep this week with straw, shredded leaves, or arborist wood chips, keeping a donut of bare soil around each stem

children.title: Fertilizer & NPK

learn.summary: The three numbers on every bag are percent nitrogen (leafy growth), phosphorus (roots and flowers), potassium (overall vigor) — so 10-10-10 is 10% of each. Excess nitrogen gives lush leaves and no fruit, and runoff pollutes waterways, so apply only what a soil test recommends. Slow-release organics (compost, fish emulsion) are far more forgiving than fast synthetics.

do: Read the NPK numbers on any fertilizer you own and check them against your soil test report before applying anything this season
